query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new integrated predictive framework that decouples lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr—by combining ML-enhanced interatomic potentials (capturing atomic-scale disorder including 1 wt.% oxygen impurities) with separate Green–Kubo molecular dynamics for phonon transport and DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations for electronic conduction—yields a total thermal conductivity prediction that is 20–30% more accurate than previous Debye-temperature or perfect-crystal based approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTaTiZr as synthesized in bulk form with inherent atomic-scale disorder and minor impurity levels (e.g., ~1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.intervention: Apply an integrated computational framework that separately calculates lattice thermal conductivity via Green–Kubo MD (using an on‐the‐fly machine-learned force field that accounts for variations in atomic mass, force constants, and defects) and electronic thermal conductivity via DFT-based Boltzmann transport, then recombines the two contributions.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) to 1200 K, with the model tailored for bulk, defected high-entropy alloys containing minor impurities.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder and point defects (including oxygen impurities) that affect local interatomic force constants and mass distributions, which in turn mediate distinct scattering mechanisms for phonons and electrons.
generation.mechanism: By training machine-learning potentials on ab initio data that inherently capture the impact of defects and disorder, the method accurately models the vibrational (phonon) transport via Green–Kubo formalism and separately the electron transport via Boltzmann theory. This decoupling prevents conflation of the two channels and accommodates temperature-dependent variations in scattering processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: The framework will predict total thermal conductivity values that agree with experiments within a 20–30% improved accuracy compared to earlier unified approaches. It will also reproduce a characteristic crossover below 200 K where lattice and electronic contributions are nearly equal, while maintaining fidelity up to 1200 K.
generation.baseline: Earlier models that use DFT-based elastic property estimations and Debye temperature approximations in perfect, defect-free bulk crystals, which conflate or approximate lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be valid for bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with typical high-entropy alloy disorder and minor (around 1 wt.%) oxygen contamination. It may not be directly applicable to nanostructured systems or samples with severe extrinsic defects beyond the examined range, and its accuracy outside 200–1200 K remains unverified.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in the precise quantitative improvement margin and in the fidelity of the decoupled predictions at very low temperatures (<200 K) where unusual scattering might occur, as well as at temperatures above 1200 K.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk samples of HfNbTaTiZr with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen content. Compute the separate lattice conductivity (using Green–Kubo MD with ML-enhanced interatomic potentials) and electronic conductivity (using DFT-based Boltzmann transport) over temperatures from below 200 K to 1200 K. Experimentally measure the total thermal conductivity alongside independent estimations of the individual contributions (for example, by electrical conductivity measurements combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law and phonon scattering spectroscopy).
measurements: Total thermal conductivity across the specified temperature range.
Temperature-dependent electronic thermal conductivity (e.g., via electrical measurements and Lorenz number evaluations).
Temperature-dependent lattice thermal conductivity (e.g., via phonon-scattering spectroscopy or other vibrational analysis).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated model does not achieve at least a 20–30% improvement in agreement with experimental total thermal conductivity values over baseline models, or if the separate trends for lattice versus electronic contributions do not exhibit the predicted crossover below 200 K and consistent behavior up to 1200 K, then the hypothesis should be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Apart from HEA, other, more conventional, types of compounds have been reported bearing low thermal conductivity, such as Zintl phases (e.g., Ba2ZnSb2 []), argyrodites [], sulfide-containing films [], rare-earth molybdates [], perovskites (e.g., []), and defective metal chalcogenide thin films [], to cite a few. Typically, the thermal conductivity of these compounds lies below 1 W/(m K). The reasons, or the conjunction of reasons, for this low thermal conductivity have been identified by means of the combined density-functional theory and Boltzmann transport theory approaches. The investigations have evidenced large Grüneisen parameters, low-lying optical and acoustic phonon frequencies, short phonon lifetime, and the presence of defects. We shall mention that, to date, several papers report on the prediction of the thermal conductivity of materials using a combined approached based on ab initio molecular dynamics used to train a machine-learned force field subsequently used with the Green–Kubo formalism to derive the heat flux and thermal conductivity [,,]. These approaches are similar to the one used in this work, which is based on the work from Verdi et al. []. It has been shown

Recently, PbSnTeSe has been experimentally investigated by Fan et al. [] and Raphel et al. [,], who report appreciably similar results for the thermoelectric performance of the material (see below). The modelling of HEAs transport properties constitute a challenge, and both the simulation methods and their derived predictions have to be confronted to experimental data to assess their validity. In this context, we present in this paper for the first time a complete approach that allows one to obtain all the transport coefficients, including the figure of merit, of a high-entropy alloy. The thermoelectric transport properties of the PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been calculated by combining state-of-the-art methods based on the special quasi-random structures approach to generate the HEA structure, the first-principles density-functional theory (DFT), and the Boltzmann transport and Green–Kubo theories. First, from the DFT-computed material electronic states, the electronic transport properties (electronic conductivity, Seebeck coefficient and electronic thermal conductivity) were calculated using the linearized Boltzmann transport equation, and the power factor was obtained. In summary, by combining first-principles calculations and on-the-fly machine learning technique with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory, the thermoelectric transport properties of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloy have been thoroughly investigated. The electronic and thermal transport coefficients of PbSnTeSe high entropy-alloy have been discussed in detail. The results indicate that PbSnTeSe has very low lattice thermal conductivities, below 0.4 W K−1 m−1. It has been found that the PF values for n-type doping are always larger than those for p-type doping because of the higher electrical conductivity. The n-type PbSnTeSe exhibits better thermoelectric properties than the p-type. The maximum ZT (≈1.1) is found at 500 K for n-type doping. These results confirm that the PbSnTeSe HEA is a promising thermoelectric (TE) material.

frame.goal: To develop a predictive model that separately quantifies and decouples lattice and electronic thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr, accurately capturing the atomic-scale complexities absent in previous perfect-crystal or simple Debye-based approaches.

decision.trend: Early work on thermal transport in concentrated alloys used analytical estimates and DFT-derived elastic properties under the assumption of perfect, defect‐free crystals. These studies often relied on Debye temperature approximations and uniform force constant models that did not account for the real atomic-scale disorder and impurities (such as 1 wt.% oxygen). More recent efforts, including the use of machine learning–enhanced interatomic potentials and atomistic simulations, have begun to incorporate defect-induced scattering and the influence of disorder. However, while such approaches have improved the accuracy of lattice (phonon) transport estimates, they still largely conflate lattice and electronic contributions or depend on integrated models that cannot separately predict the two transport channels across the full temperature range.
decision.unsolved: A predictive model that separately decouples and quantifies lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr—accurately capturing the effects of atomic-scale disorder and minor impurities over the regime of <200 K (where contributions are comparable) to 1200 K—has not yet been achieved.
decision.lever: integrated ML-enhanced interatomic potential combined with separate transport channels: applying Green–Kubo molecular dynamics for phonon (lattice) conductivity alongside DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations for the electronic conduction
decision.why: Building on the trend, this approach directly addresses the deficiencies of earlier idealized and Debye-based models by incorporating atomic-scale disorder (including realistic oxygen impurity levels) via machine learning potentials. By decoupling the lattice and electronic channels, it provides separate, testable predictions for each contribution. The hypothesis would be that, for HfNbTaTiZr, this method yields a roughly 20–30% improvement in predicting total thermal conductivity relative to experiments, with a characteristic crossover below 200 K (where lattice and electronic contributions are of similar magnitude) and sustained accuracy up to 1200 K. Decisive falsification would occur if experimental measurements at low and high temperatures do not reflect the predicted separate trends or if the predicted improvement, quantified by comparisons to both impurity-free and 1 wt.% oxygen samples, is not observed.
